Repudiate

rih-PYOO-dee-ayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To repudiate to formally reject or disown something, often as false or unacceptable.

After decades of silence, the aging author finally repudiated the offensive views expressed in his early novels.

Worked Example

When evidence surfaced that the charity's founder had misused donations, the board publicly repudiated him and cut all remaining ties.

To repudiate someone or something is to formally and firmly reject it, often to distance yourself from something shameful or false.

How Repudiate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

disown

disown: to refuse to accept as one's own

reject: to refuse to accept or believe something

Antonyms

endorse

endorse: to publicly express approval or support

embrace

embrace: to accept something readily and enthusiastically

How Strong Is It? — doubt → repudiate → renounce

doubt vs. repudiate

doubt vs. repudiate: To doubt something is a mild uncertainty, far short of formally rejecting it.

renounce vs. repudiate

renounce vs. repudiate: To renounce something is to formally give up your own claim to it entirely, an even more total act than rejecting someone else's claim.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back, away (Latin)

root — pudiare

root — pudiare: to cast off (from repudium, 'divorce') (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Repudiate traces back to Latin repudiare, 'to cast off or divorce,' from repudium, an ancient legal term for a formal divorce announcement. Its deeper root is debated by scholars, so there's no common modern English word to quiz you on here -- just this one fascinating historical cousin.

Use the root in a new word: repudium

Use the root in a new word: repudium: In ancient Rome, a husband could end a marriage simply by declaring a repudium in front of witnesses.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Repudiate is a strong, formal word -- reserve it for firmly and publicly rejecting a claim, belief, debt, or relationship, not for everyday disagreement. It's a closer relative of renege (breaking a personal promise) and rescind (officially cancelling a law, contract, or policy) than it might first appear -- all three describe 'going back' on something, just at different levels of formality.
